blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand HTML Lists and Tables

Welcome to Lesson 5: HTML Lists and Tables. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “HTML Lists and Tables”. The goal is to ordered lists, unordered lists, nested lists, tables, rows, columns and table structure.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Use lists for grouped items and tables for genuinely tabular relationships between row and column headers. Tables need a clear header structure so users can understand what each value represents.

blocks.question: A price list has values associated with column headings. What makes the table easier to interpret?
options: Use header cells and a clear row/column structure.
Put everything in one giant cell.
Use bold paragraphs instead of rows.
Remove all headings.
blocks.explanation: Header cells communicate the relationship between labels and data cells.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Header cells communicate the relationship between labels and data cells.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Header cells communicate the relationship between labels and data cells.

blocks.title: Sample 2: HTML Lists and Tables in practice

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real HTML project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A page lists three steps in a process. Which structure is best?
options: A table with blank cells.
An ordered list.
A form with required fields.
A video without controls.
blocks.explanation: A numbered sequence is most naturally represented by an ordered list.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A numbered sequence is most naturally represented by an ordered list.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A numbered sequence is most naturally represented by an ordered list.

blocks.text: Nested lists can express hierarchy, but keep nesting shallow enough to remain readable. In tables, use header cells for headings and add a caption when it clarifies the table’s purpose.

blocks.title: Sample 3: HTML Lists and Tables in practice

blocks.question: A wide data table overflows a phone screen. What should the developer consider?
options: Hide the headings.
Make every cell one character wide.
Provide a responsive strategy, such as a scrollable container or alternative view.
Remove the data from the page.
blocks.explanation: Wide tables need a mobile strategy that preserves access to the information.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Wide tables need a mobile strategy that preserves access to the information.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Wide tables need a mobile strategy that preserves access to the information.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
On small screens, wide tables may need a horizontal scroll container or a different presentation. Do not use tables merely to position the page layout.

blocks.text: Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Present structured information clearly using lists and tables. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.

blocks.question: A list contains a value at the first position. In a zero-based language, which index usually addresses it?
options: One.
The collection length.
Zero.
Minus one.
blocks.explanation: Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
